title.zh: 喀布尔沦陷五年：塔利班庆祝，澳大利亚哀叹

Meanwhile, Australia, the United Nations, and human rights groups highlight a deepening humanitarian crisis and systematic repression of women.

In Kabul, white flags of the Islamic Emirate adorned streets alongside decorated US military vehicles left behind during the chaotic 2021 withdrawal.

Taliban authorities hosted sports matches — from which women are barred — to commemorate their takeover, asserting that independence has brought national security and economic stability.

Taliban government chief spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said authorities were laying the "foundations of the economy" and appealed for patience.

"Five years on from the fall of Kabul, our thoughts are with the people of Afghanistan, who continue to face violent repression at the hands of the Taliban, as well as the Afghan community in Australia and around the world," the statement read.

The government leaders honored the service of more than 39,000 Australian Defence Force and civilian personnel who served in Afghanistan over two decades, remembering the 41 soldiers who died during operations and those lost after returning home.

The statement noted that Australia has provided $310 million in direct aid through non-government channels since September 2021, while establishing an autonomous sanctions framework against senior Taliban figures and backing international action under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW).

"Australia has not stepped back from that responsibility," ministers stated, pointing to expanded migration pathways for displaced Afghans and ongoing support for locally engaged Afghan employees now living in Australia.

title.en: 'I've never seen scenes like this': Why Britain is burning
title.zh: 英国为何“火光冲天”？

summary.en: Wildfires have devastated homes across Britain, prompting Prime Minister Andy Burnham to advocate for a clean energy transition to address the country's vulnerability to such events.
summary.zh: 英国各地野火肆虐，摧毁了许多房屋，促使首相安迪·伯纳姆呼吁向清洁能源转型，以应对该国在此类事件中的脆弱性。

body.en:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Friday that Britain must face up to the reality of the changing climate and accelerate its move to clean energy as he visited a town gutted by wildfire.

In Stourbridge, near the UK's second-largest city of Birmingham, smoke rose from smouldering ruins of several roofless houses as firefighters sprayed water on the wreckage.

The West Midlands Fire Service said 19 houses were completely destroyed and 18 others damaged in the town.

Meeting firefighters there after viewing the scene, Burnham said the "combustible situation" was related to climate change and showed the need for a more rapid clean energy transition.

"I've never seen scenes like this in Britain, where you just see a whole house gutted, smouldering," he said.

"We have to face up to the changing climate ... there's no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy."

Burnham — who took power last month — has faced criticism for not directly referencing climate change sooner, as Britain, like much of Europe, has grappled for weeks with widespread drought, extreme heat, and wildfires.

The UK has set a target to consume zero carbon-based electricity by 2030 and is aiming to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 to combat climate change.

Describing Britain as "a tinderbox" with 37 blazes nationwide on Friday, the prime minister warned against lighting fires outdoors, as the government introduced a ban on selling disposable barbecue equipment.

People across England and Wales began receiving a rare emergency alert on their phones from 7:00pm local time, warning them not to light "anything that could spark a fire, including barbecues, campfires, and fireworks".

Residents of Stourbridge were evacuated, and some were treated for smoke inhalation after the fire there spread on Thursday, the UK's hottest day of the year so far. Temperatures reached a high of 38.1C in west London.

One firefighter was hospitalised and five others suffered minor injuries, the fire service confirmed, with crews continuing to extinguish "hotspots" in open grassland, along a railway and in gardens.

Six other firefighters farther north in Staffordshire were taken to hospital suffering from smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion battling similar blazes there, the fire service said.

The ambulance service in the West Midlands region, including Stourbridge and Staffordshire, said it had treated 68 people Thursday with symptoms such as smoke inhalation, 25 of whom were hospitalised.

summary.en: Donald Trump announced his intention to declare the Strait of Hormuz as US territory following a defeat of Iran. This statement comes as gas prices have risen significantly after Iran closed the strait in response to US and Israeli attacks.

body.en:
Donald Trump said the strait would become part of the US after Iran is defeated. He also told Americans to accept higher gas prices, which have soared since Iran closed Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks.

President Donald Trump said Friday that he would "soon" declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory.

"After we finish defeating Iran , which is being very badly defeated — pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States," Trump said at a rally at a police academy in Garden City, New York state. "It's true," he added.

It was not clear whether his remarks were serious or whether they signal a new policy shift for Washington in its war against Tehran , which is more than five months old.

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi dismissed Trump's remarks, saying the country would "not be intimidated" and that the strategic waterway would remain under its control and authority.

The US and Israel launched the war against Iran on February 28. At the time, senior White House officials, including Trump, said the aim was to end Iran's nuclear program and spark a popular uprising to force regime change in the Islamic Republic, among other goals.

Iran's response has been to target US allies across the Middle East with drone and missile strikes, as well as to impose a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments passed before the war.

The US responded to Iran's closure of the strait with its own naval blockade of Iranian ships and ports. The two countries have been locked in a stalemate over the vital waterway for months, causing energy prices to soar.

Rising oil and gas costs and the economic fallout from the war are likely to be leading issues in the midterm elections in November.

During the rally, the US president also urged Americans to accept that they would have to "pay a tiny little bit more" for their gasoline as a worthy price for preventing "a very evil country" from getting a nuclear weapon.

"What we're doing is a great service for the world, not only for ourselves ... and we're really doing a ​great job," Trump told the crowd, adding that "no ships get through (the US blockade of Hormuz) unless we want them to."

On Friday, Trump also dismissed concerns over the living conditions aboard a US aircraft carrier that was deployed to the Middle East amid the war with Iran.

Relatives of service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln told US military media outlets that personnel are struggling with difficult living conditions and deteriorating mental health . There have also been reports of suicide attempts.

title.en: Trump asks Supreme Court to let White House ballroom construction continue
title.zh: 特朗普请求最高法院允许白宫宴会厅项目继续施工

summary.en: Justice Department lawyers supported the US president's assertion that the $400 million White House ballroom project is essential for security, as the president asked the Supreme Court to allow its construction to proceed.
summary.zh: 司法部律师支持美国总统的说法，即耗资4亿美元的白宫宴会厅项目是出于安全需要，此前总统已请求最高法院允许该项目继续施工。

body.en:
Justice Department lawyers echoed the US president's claim that the $400 million White House ballroom ​project is a security necessity.

The Trump administration on Friday asked the US Supreme Court to allow construction to continue on the president's $400 million White House ballroom.

It comes a week after an appeals court ruled Donald Trump's ballroom project, planned for the site of the White House's East Wing after it was demolished, lacked congressional approval and ordered above-ground construction to stop .

"This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security," Trump's Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in a petition to the Supreme Court.

Chief Justice John Roberts set a deadline of Tuesday for a response by plaintiffs challenging the ballroom project.

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation first brought the case after the East Wing was torn down and work began on a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom.

In a 2-1 ruling on August 7, the DC Circuit upheld a lower-court judge's order directing the administration to halt above-ground construction.

"Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide and is not a matter for Executive self-help," the appeals court panel wrote.

To justify the need for a secure ballroom, Justice Department lawyers pointed to the July 8 missile threat against Air Force One when Trump was flown out of Turkey aboard a secret flight and other recent assassination attempts.

The filing also claims the project is on time and under budget, funded by about $400 million in private donations. Democrats, however, say Trump's tax law is helping pay for the ballroom, while lawmakers in Congress have not approved a request by the administration for additional funding.

Responding to the petition, the trust accused the White House of trying to "outrun the courts" by accelerating construction. It cited plans to install 1 million pounds (453,592.37 kilograms) of rebarand pour 3,000 cubic yards (81,000 cubic feet, 2,293.66 cubic meters) of concrete over the next week.

"The Administration's transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review, and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here," the plaintiffs said.

The National Trust has urged the Supreme Court to reject the administration's appeal.

title.en: 'I shot Mr Thompson': Luigi Mangione pleads guilty in US CEO murder trial
title.zh: “我枪杀了汤普森先生”：路易吉·曼吉奥内在美国首席执行官谋杀案审判中认罪

summary.en: Luigi Mangione has pleaded guilty in the murder trial of a US CEO. His legal team is now working to dismiss parallel state murder charges against him.
summary.zh: 路易吉·曼吉奥内在美国首席执行官谋杀案审判中认罪。他的律师团队目前正努力驳回针对其当事人的平行州谋杀指控。

body.en:
Luigi Mangione has admitted to gunning down a top United States health insurance boss in a Manhattan street as he pleaded guilty to stalking charges before a federal judge.

In a crime that shook corporate America and gripped the world , 28-year-old Mangione is alleged to have murdered chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, Brian Thompson, 50, in December 2024 in a protest against the US health insurance system.

"On the morning of December 4, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione told a federal judge.

Mangione will be sentenced on 18 December and prosecutors have said they will seek a life term.

He had been facing the stalking charges in the federal system, alongside murder charges in the New York state system, but Mangione's lawyers have now called for the state charges to be dropped to prevent him being prosecuted twice for the same conduct.

"We just filed our motion in state court, explaining why the state charges must be dismissed under New York's double jeopardy protections," said Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo.

The stalking charges and the murder charges could both lead to life sentences. Two other federal charges that carried the death penalty were thrown out by a judge earlier this year.

The case has sharply divided already polarized public opinion, with conservatives led by US President Donald Trump calling for an example to be made of Mangione.

"There can be no celebrity in assassination," Jamie McDonald, the US attorney for the Southern District of New York, told reporters.

But ardent supporters of Mangione flocked to the Manhattan courthouse to show their support amid heavy security as a helicopter hovered overhead.

Relatives of Thompson were in court for the hearing, and a man shouted "America loves Luigi" at them as they left in a convoy of black SUVs.

"While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable," the family said in a statement after the hearing.

They noted that the murder trial was still to come and said they would "continue to seek the justice" Thompson deserved.

Thompson's murder raised deep public frustration with the lucrative US commercial health care system, with some social media users painting Mangione as a hero.

He was arrested in Altoona, Pennsylvania, on 9 December following a tip from staff at a McDonald's restaurant, after a days-long manhunt.

He had traveled to New York by bus from Atlanta about 10 days before the crime, US prosecutors said.

title.en: It was a moment that stunned the world. Now, it's testing the limits of the US' power
title.zh: 这是一个震惊世界的时刻。现在，它正在考验美国权力的极限

summary.en: Nicolás Maduro's capture and transfer to a US courtroom has sparked a global debate among experts regarding the boundaries of US power and the appropriate application of international law in such cases.
summary.zh: 尼古拉斯·马杜罗被捕并被移送至美国法庭一事，引发了全球专家关于美国权力界限以及国际法在此类案件中如何适用的激烈辩论。

body.en:
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.

Less than a month after a former president serving time in a United States federal prison was released, another foreign leader was captured and indicted.

Their cases bear some striking similarities. Both were presidents targeted by US authorities in drug trafficking-related offences. Both ultimately found themselves in the US justice system. And in an unlikely coincidence, both were held at the same federal detention facility in Brooklyn, New York.

The sliding doors moment came in January when Maduro was captured — four years after Hernández was imprisoned , and just two months after Hernández was unexpectedly pardoned by US President Donald Trump.

Maduro's case now places two very different paths to a US courtroom side by side: one through extradition and prosecution after a president leaves office, the other through a military operation that removed a sitting leader from his own country.

Unlike Hernández, Maduro was captured while still Venezuela's president in a US military operation and flown directly to New York. Hernández, by contrast, was arrested after leaving office and extradited to the US through formal legal proceedings.

That distinction has put questions of sovereignty, head-of-state immunity and the limits of US power at the centre of Maduro's prosecution.

Maduro was first elected president in 2013, winning by a narrow margin in an election his opponents disputed. He remained in power through two further presidential terms, amid repeated allegations of electoral irregularities and repression.

The US has long accused Maduro and senior members of his government of facilitating cocaine trafficking through Venezuela . US prosecutors have alleged Venezuelan officials used state institutions and their positions of power to provide protection and logistical support to drug-trafficking organisations.

Maduro has repeatedly denied the allegations and described the US case as politically motivated.

He faces four federal criminal counts: narco-terrorism conspiracy, conspiracy to import cocaine, possession of machine guns and destructive devices, and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. He has pleaded not guilty .

The charges carry lengthy potential prison terms, including a possible life sentence if Maduro is convicted on the narco-terrorism charge.

title.en: Dozens injured and thousands evacuated in Croatia wildfire
title.zh: 克罗地亚野火致数十人受伤，数千人撤离

summary.en: Officials report that a massive wildfire near the port town of Omis, Croatia, has injured dozens and forced the evacuation of thousands, marking it as one of the country's most severe blazes in history.
summary.zh: 官员称，克罗地亚港口城镇奥米什附近发生的大规模野火已造成数十人受伤，数千人撤离，这是该国历史上最严重的火灾之一。

body.en:
At least one person has died and around 40 others have been injured after a severe wildfire tore through cities on Croatia's coastline on Thursday night and Friday morning.

The blaze broke out near the village of Lokva Rogoznica on Thursday evening, and spread quickly towards the nearby tourist town of Omis, 6km (7 miles) away.

Around 1,200 residents and tourists were evacuated, while 10 people were in intensive care in hospital, the prime minister said. Croatia's fire chief Slavko Tucakovic described it as "one of the worst" blazes in the country's history.

Croatia is one of several European nations suffering devastating wildfires , after a summer of extreme heat and dry conditions.

Villages near the Adriatic city of Split were struck by the blaze, which coursed through pine forest-lined hillside, causing extensive damage to homes and cars.

Tucakovic said the firestorm burned through "everything in their path" as officials confirmed flames, fanned by strong winds, engulfed 1,000 hectares in just four hours.

More than 300 firefighters were deployed overnight on Thursday, with crews sometimes forced to retreat as the fire advanced.

Footage shared online shows thick smoke and huge flames tearing through surrounding vegetation, turning the sky red, as stranded residents and tourists looked on.

Emergency shelters were opened in several towns along the coast, as evacuations continued throughout the night.

On Friday, officials confirmed that a body had been discovered in a burnt-out area as emergency services continued searching affected zones.

Later on Friday, Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic visited the affected area, where he praised the work of emergency crews.

The fire had spread at "lightning speed" and with "gale-force winds", he told reporters, adding that what firefighters had managed to save was "truly a miracle".

The Commander of Omis Volunteer Fire Department, Viseslav Pesic told Reuters the blaze was so intense that people had abandoned vehicles "directly in the fire zone", making it difficult for emergency crews to pass through.

Firefighters across Europe have been facing intense pressure and a strain on resources as serious wildfires continue to rage across the continent, fuelled by extreme heatwaves.

In Agios Vasileios in Greece, more than 200 people were evacuated by boat from a beach resort after wildfires raged across the country, while more than 500 residents were forced to leave their homes because of a fire in the south-western Landes region, near to an area already devastated by wildfires.

More than 2,000 people were also evacuated from the village of Gey in western Germany after a forest fire spread towards a village near the Belgian border.

body.zh: 周四晚上和周五早上，一场严重的野火席卷了克罗地亚海岸线的城市，造成至少 1 人死亡、约 40 人受伤。 周四晚上，大火在 Lokva Rogoznica 村附近爆发，并迅速蔓延至 6 公里（7 英里）外的附近旅游小镇奥米斯。 总理表示，约 1,200 名居民和游客被疏散，另有 10 人在医院接受重症监护。克罗地亚消防队长斯拉夫科·图卡科维奇称这是该国历史上“最严重的”火灾之一。 在经历了夏季的极度炎热和干燥之后，克罗地亚是遭受毁灭性野火袭击的几个欧洲国家之一。 亚得里亚海城市斯普利特附近的村庄遭到大火袭击，大火蔓延到松林成荫的山坡上，对房屋和汽车造成大面积损坏。 图卡科维奇表示，这场大火烧毁了“沿途的一切”，官员们证实，强风助长的火焰在短短四个小时内就吞噬了 1,000 公顷土地。 周四连夜部署了 300 多名消防员，随着火势蔓延，消防人员有时被迫撤退。 网上分享的视频显示，浓烟和巨大的火焰撕裂了周围的植被，将天空染红，滞留的居民和游客在一旁观看。 沿海几个城镇开设了紧急避难所，疏散工作整夜持续进行。 周五，官员们证实，紧急服务部门继续搜寻受影响地区，在烧毁的地区发现了一具尸体。 周五晚些时候，克罗地亚总理安德烈·普连科维奇访问了受影响地区，并赞扬了应急人员的工作。 他告诉记者，火势以“闪电般的速度”和“强风”蔓延，并补充说，消防队员成功拯救的东西“确实是一个奇迹”。 奥米斯志愿消防队指挥官维塞斯拉夫·佩西奇告诉路透社，火势非常猛烈，人们“直接将车辆遗弃在火区”，导致紧急救援人员难以通过。 由于严重的野火在极端热浪的推动下继续在整个欧洲大陆肆虐，欧洲各地的消防员一直面临着巨大的压力和资源紧张。 在希腊的阿吉奥斯瓦西里奥斯，全国山火肆虐后，超过200人从海滩度假胜地乘船撤离，而西南部朗德地区发生火灾，超过500名居民被迫离开家园，该地区靠近已经被山火摧毁的地区。 森林大火蔓延至比利时边境附近的一个村庄后，德国西部盖伊村的 2000 多人也被疏散。 与此同时，紧急野火警报已向数百万人发出……

reflection.en: As wildfires rage and communities face displacement and injury, the immediate need for safety and support is profound. Psalm 46:1 reminds us that Yahweh is our refuge and strength, a very present help in times of trouble. In such moments of crisis, we can lean on divine strength and find solace in community solidarity.

verse.textZh: 神是我们的避难所，是我们的力量，是我们在患难中随时的帮助。

title.en: Jason Arday: Ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism scandal found dead
title.zh: 杰森·阿尔戴：抄袭丑闻中心的前剑桥教授被发现死亡

summary.en: Jason Arday, the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge, was found unresponsive at an address in London. Arday had recently resigned in the midst of a plagiarism row.
summary.zh: 这是一则来自全球栏目的新闻，重点涉及和平与克制。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
Jason Arday, the youngest ever Black professor at Cambridge, was found unresponsive at an address in London. Arday had recently resigned in the midst of a plagiarism row.

Jason Arday, the former University of Cambridge professor who resigned amid allegations of plagiarism, was found dead on Friday.

Without naming him directly, the Metropolitan Police said he was found "unresponsive" in Battersea, south London , and pronounced dead at the scene.

"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," a spokesperson said. "His next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by officers."

Arday, a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, one of the world's top universities, resigned just over a week ago amid mounting allegations that he plagiarized parts of his PhD thesis and overstated his personal achievements.

He had denied wrongdoing, saying in a resignation letter last week that he did not accept "the narratives that have surrounded me."

British newspapers and commentators have seized on the allegations, arguing that he gained an unfair advantage through diversity, equality and inclusion (DEI) policies.

Scrutiny of Arday's credentials intensified last month after criticism from former Cambridge researcher Nathan Cofnas.

The Times of London later reported similarities between passages in Arday's 2015 PhD thesis and an earlier paper by another researcher.

Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated and cleared by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.

But last week, Cambridge launched an investigation following "new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."

British media also questioned Arday's claims of having raised £5.5 million (€6.4 million, $7.4 million) for charity through endurance challenges. Arday told The Guardian the funds were raised collectively over two decades.

Supporters, including over two dozen academics and politicians, characterized the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to discredit Arday and other Black people in influential positions.

In his resignation letter, Arday said that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."

His family issued a statement denouncing the "campaign of sustained abuse" Arday had faced since he took the role at Cambridge University more than three years ago.

"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," Arday's family said.

reflection.en: This story draws attention to peace-making and restraint. Matthew 5:9 reminds us to meet sharp headlines with mercy, truth, and restraint, asking how faithful people can respond with wisdom instead of noise.

title.en: Mangione admits killing healthcare CEO and pleads guilty to federal charges
title.zh: 曼吉奥内承认杀害医疗保健公司首席执行官并对联邦指控认罪

summary.en: A 28-year-old man, Mangione, has admitted to killing a healthcare CEO in Manhattan and pleaded guilty to federal charges of stalking resulting in death. He stated, "I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died."
summary.zh: 28岁的曼吉奥内承认在曼哈顿杀害了一名医疗保健公司首席执行官，并对导致死亡的跟踪指控表示认罪。他表示：“我在曼哈顿枪杀了汤普森先生，他死了。”

body.en:
Luigi Mangione has admitted to killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson after pleading guilty to federal charges of interstate stalking resulting in death.

"I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died," the 28-year-old admitted in Manhattan federal court on Friday.

Thompson, a 50-year-old father of two , was shot from behind on 4 December, 2024 as he walked into a hotel in midtown Manhattan. Following the plea hearing, his family issued a statement calling it "an important step toward justice for Brian and for our family".

Mangione faces a maximum sentence of life in prison. He also faces state charges , although his lawyers are seeking to get those dismissed following his guilty plea.

Mangione had initially pleaded not guilty in both the federal and state cases against him for the shooting death of Thompson.

At a hearing in Manhattan federal court on Friday, Mangione's lawyers announced that he intended to plead guilty to the two federal charges against him.

Wearing a beige prison outfit, Mangione appeared solemn and serious throughout the hearing.

Reading a statement aloud to the court, he admitted to planning the attack ahead of time, crossing state lines with the intent to kill and using a gun he printed on a 3-D-printer and equipped with a silencer and magazine.

He told the court he was driven to kill Thompson because of his experience with the healthcare system "after years of enduring severe pains from a broken back".

Mangione stated that he had learned UnitedHealthcare would hold an annual investor conference in Manhattan in December 2024.

He also said he emailed UnitedHealthcare prior to the conference "posing as an investor" and asking questions about the event.

"I emailed UnitedHealthcare with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson," Mangione said in his statement. "On the morning of Dec. 4, 2024 I shot Mr. Thompson in Manhattan in his back."

Thompson's family said in a statement that they will continue to seek justice in both New York state and Pennsylvania, where Mangione was arrested .

"While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable.

"Now we look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family added.

Prosecutors have recommended Mangione serve between 24-30 years in prison. But Judge Margaret Garnett said in court that she ultimately decides his sentence.

title.en: Trump asks Supreme Court to allow ballroom work to continue
title.zh: 特朗普要求最高法院允许宴会厅工程继续进行

summary.en: The US administration has appealed to the Supreme Court, requesting permission to continue work on a ballroom project. The administration argued that requiring the president to seek approval from Congress for such work would be "dangerous."

body.en:
US President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to allow him to continue building a $400m (£295m) ballroom at the White House without congressional permission.

The emergency application comes one week after an appeals court ordered construction to stop until Congress approves, upholding a ruling won by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued the administration last year.

In the latest filing, US Solicitor General D John Sauer asked that work be allowed to continue while the administration appeals the stop-work order, which he called "dangerous".

Trump has long argued the White House lacks a large event space and that building one is vital for national security.

Last week's appeals court decision does not take effect until 21 August, when ballroom construction will have to cease unless the Supreme Court grants the emergency application.

Sauer said in the filing on Friday that work on the project is 65% done and not granting it would amount to "construction-by-injunction".

"With the dangerous injunction poised to take effect for the first time on August 21, its stop-work mandate is even more flagrantly inequitable, if not impossible," he wrote.

Sauer added that "forcing the president to come hat-in-hand to Congress so the people's house is safe gives the legislature dangerous leverage".

Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts ordered the National Trust for Historic Preservation to file a response by noon on Tuesday.

Trump's ballroom project has been the subject of a legal battle since October, when the administration demolished the East Wing of the White House to begin construction without congressional approval.

Soon after, the Trust filed a lawsuit arguing that the project was unlawful because it began without a legally required review, which also includes public comment and approval by entities such as the National Capital Planning Commission.

In a statement following Friday's emergency application, the Trust accused the administration of "refusing to listen" to previous rulings and "actively attempting to outrun the courts by accelerating construction of the ballroom".

"The administration's transparent efforts to evade the rule of law, frustrate judicial review and limit the availability of meaningful relief in the courts must stop here," the statement added.

The president and the government's lawyers have argued that in addition to the ballroom to host events, the project also includes military facilities, including bomb shelters and centres for medical treatment.

The administration has also argued that the ballroom is being constructed without any taxpayer money and is fully funded by private corporate donations - meaning that Congressional approval is not required.

title.en: Afghan women tell the BBC their lives are unrecognisable after five years of Taliban rule

summary.en: Women across the country speak of public floggings, losing their jobs, and barriers to healthcare that endanger lives.

body.en:
Five years on from the Taliban takeover in Afghanistan, women and girls have told the BBC their lives are unrecognisable under the rule of the regime.

The hard-line Islamist group has been eroding the rights of the 22 million women in the country since it re-gained control in 2021- two decades after being removed from power by a US-led military coalition.

The BBC is one of the few media organisations that has been able to maintain access to Afghanistan since the takeover. We spoke to women across the country, from the heart of Kabul to the vast countryside.

They have watched on as the Taliban barred access to school for girls over 12, restricted travel without a male chaperone and brought in a law implying legal approval for child marriage.

When questioned by BBC Afghan over the constraints that women face, the Taliban's foreign minister said: "Women are not totally restricted on all walks of life".

But the restrictions impact almost every part of their lives and make it difficult to tell their stories. Many of the women have not used their real names because they fear reprisals.

"People are so overwhelmed by poverty and daily hardships that many have been forced to put their education, dreams, and hopes for the future aside," Ela from Kabul said.

"Today, survival has become the priority, and many of us no longer have the time or energy to think about the future."

Afghanistan is currently the only country in the world where girls are officially banned from secondary and higher education.

Shakiba recounted that "15 August, when the government fell, was the worst and most painful day of my life.

"Every year when this date comes I feel as if an old wound opens again and a new feeling of defeat fills my heart.

"That day I felt that many of the dreams I had carried inside me for years were suddenly taken away."

Though Shakiba has managed to finish her secondary education online - "a very important victory" - she says her life-long goal of becoming a pilot feels impossible.

"Whenever I looked at the sky I imagined myself flying an airplane and seeing the world from above. I wanted to fly freely and experience a world without limits," she said.

The Taliban's foreign minister, Amir Khan Muttaqi, was asked by the BBC about education for girls in Afghanistan, specifically referencing a Unicef report stating that around 2.6 million girls in the country are now unable to attend school beyond Grade 6.

Amir Khan Muttaqi replied that "it is not correct to say everything is banned for women", adding that "right now, three million girls are going to schools and madrassas [religious centres focused on Islamic teachings]".

title.en: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges in Brian Thompson death
title.zh: 路易吉·曼吉奥尼 (Luigi Mangione) 承认联邦跟踪布莱恩·汤普森 (Brian Thompson) 之死的罪名

summary.en: The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.
summary.zh: 这是一则来自全球栏目的新闻，重点涉及公义、尊严与问责。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
The plea resolves the remaining federal charges tied to the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson and could affect a separate New York state case.

Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty in a Manhattan federal court to stalking charges tied to the death of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson .

Prosecutors said Mangione traveled to New York City and fatally shot Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel on December 4, 2024, as he walked to UnitedHealth Group's annual investor conference. 

The judge has accepted his guilty plea and said sentencing would take place in December. Mangione faces a possible sentence ‌of life without parole on the two counts of stalking.

Mangione had previously pleaded not guilty to federal murder, weapons and stalking charges. Earlier this year, the judge dismissed the murder and weapons counts on legal technicalities, leaving only the stalking charges and eliminating the possibility of the death penalty.

Mangione still seperately  faces murder, weapons and forgery charges in New York state court. 

Outside federal court, Mangione's lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, told reporters that "state charges must be dismissed under New York's double jeopardy protections."

Under double jeopardy protections, defendants are protected from being prosecuted for the same crime twice.

Mangione told the federal court he pursued Thompson "after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system."

Thompson was chief executive of UnitedHealthcare, one of the largest health insurers in the United States .

He was walking into a Midtown Manhattan hotel for the annual investor day when he was shot three times in the back.

Mangione said he then used a 3D printer to make part of the gun used in the shooting.

The killing underscored widespread frustration with the US healthcare system, and some supporters portrayed Mangione as a hero.

Conservatives, including President Donald Trump, however, have called for a tough punishment.

Jamie McDonald, the Manhattan US attorney, told reporters that his office would seek a sentence of life imprisonment.

Outside the courthouse, a man shouted "America loves Luigi" at relatives of Thompson as they left court Friday in a convoy of black SUVs.

Thompson's family said in a statement that the plea marked an "important step toward justice."

"We look to the court to ensure that sentencing reflects the severity of this crime," the family said.

title.en: The major citizenship ruling affecting Australians like Ophelia
title.zh: 影响奥菲莉亚等澳大利亚人的重大公民身份裁决

summary.en: A landmark court ruling in Australia is expected to alter the criteria and possibilities for citizenship claims for certain individuals within the country.
summary.zh: 澳大利亚一项具有里程碑意义的法院裁决，可能会重塑该国部分公民的公民身份申请条件和可能性。

body.en:
When Ophelia Bryant first travelled to Italy in 1986, she says she felt something she could not quite explain.

Her parents had been born in Italy, as had all four of her grandparents. They immigrated to Australia in 1955, where Bryant was born three years later.

Italy has remained a constant in her life, with Bryant returning more than a dozen times to visit relatives and reconnect with her family roots.

But when she began looking into whether she could formally claim Italian citizenship, she discovered her family history came with a legal complication.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Her parents became Australian citizens in 1961, when Bryant was a child, and later formally renounced their Italian citizenship.

Under a restrictive interpretation of Italy's citizenship laws, known as the 'minor issue', that could break the line of citizenship transmission.

Now, a landmark decision by Italy's highest court has changed that legal interpretation — and Bryant is "optimistic because that door may finally be open".

The so-called minor issue arose from conflicting interpretations of Italy's 1912 citizenship law.

One provision established that children born overseas to an Italian citizen could acquire Italian citizenship from birth.

Another was interpreted as meaning that when an Italian parent became a citizen of another country, their minor children could lose their Italian citizenship along with them.

That interpretation gained ground through Italian court decisions from 2023 onwards, leading to the rejection of citizenship-by-descent applications.

But in July, Italy's Supreme Court's United Sections, the court's highest panel for resolving conflicting legal interpretations, ruled that citizenship acquired at birth was not automatically lost when an Italian parent subsequently naturalised in another country.

Brisbane-based Italian lawyer Fabrizio Fiorino, who advises clients on Italian citizenship applications, said the decision effectively restores the previous interpretation of the law.

"It was not a change in a provision, but it was a change in the interpretation of rules," he said.

He told SBS News the ruling means people who were Italian citizens from birth cannot simply be considered to have lost that citizenship because their parents later became foreign citizens while they were minors.

For thousands of people whose citizenship applications were rejected on that basis, the decision could provide a pathway back.

Italy's interior ministry has since issued a letter instructing authorities to follow the Supreme Court's interpretation.

title.en: US says dozens of countries helped China dodge Trump's tariffs
title.zh: 美国称数十个国家帮助中国规避特朗普关税

summary.en: A new US report indicates that China utilized various countries with lower tariffs to reroute goods, thereby avoiding higher levies imposed by the Trump administration.
summary.zh: 一份新的美国报告指出，中国通过关税较低的国家转运货物，以规避特朗普政府征收的更高关税。

body.en:
The White House said in a report on Thursday that more than 40 countries had helped China sidestep US tariffs by routing exports through nations that face lower American import duties.

The countries named include Canada, India, Mexico, Japan and South Korea, which the White House said had helped China evade tens of billions of dollars in tariffs, which are levied on companies importing goods.

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro said it had cost "American jobs and billions in revenue".

A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington said "trade wars have no winners" and that it opposes the US tariff measures and the use of state power to target China's companies.

"Any unilateral actions or agreements concerning transshipped goods must not target or harm the interests of third parties," the spokesperson added.

The BBC has contacted the US embassies of Canada, India, Mexico, Japan, South Korea and other trading partners listed in the report for comment.

The report follows a wave of sanctions between the US and China and comes weeks before US President Donald Trump will meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington.

Between $30bn (£22bn) and roughly $300bn in goods have been moved from countries with higher tariffs through those with lower rates, according to government and private sector estimates quoted by the White House.

The process is known as transshipping, which refers to the practice of transferring cargo through another country while en route to a final destination.

The US accused China of "taking advantage" of the practice by moving goods through nations that have lower import duties.

China has used third countries as a stopover and has repackaged goods to hide their real origin to obtain lower tariffs, the White House said in its report, describing the process as "fraud cloaked in paperwork".

"What has changed in today's Great Transshipment Scam is not merely the speed and scale of this modern form of smuggling, but the breadth, depth, and sophistication of the global Shadow Transshipment Network through which China's tariff evasion now moves," the White House wrote.

The US has deployed artificial intelligence tools to catch transshipment efforts, it added.

The report is expected to add to key sticking points between the sides as Trump and Xi prepare to meet in the US in September, and Chang Pao Li, associate professor of economics at Singapore Management University, said it could be used to strengthen the US bargaining position.

"Washington can argue that China has preserved access to the US market indirectly and that any broader trade settlement must therefore address not only direct Chinese exports but also third-country routing," she told the BBC.

body.zh: 白宫周四在一份报告中表示，已有 40 多个国家通过美国进口关税较低的国家进行出口，帮助中国规避美国关税。 被点名的国家包括加拿大、印度、墨西哥、日本和韩国，白宫称这些国家帮助中国逃避了数百亿美元的关税。 白宫贸易顾问彼得·纳瓦罗表示，这损失了“美国的就业机会和数十亿美元的收入”。 中国驻华盛顿大使馆发言人在回应BBC询问时表示，“贸易战没有赢家”，反对美国采取关税措施，反对动用国家力量针对中国企业。 该发言人补充说，“任何涉及转运货物的单方面行动或协议均不得针对或损害第三方利益。” BBC已联系加拿大、印度、墨西哥、日本、韩国和报告中列出的其他贸易伙伴的美国大使馆征求评论。 该报告是在美国和中国之间实施一波制裁之后发布的，几周前唐纳德·特朗普总统将在华盛顿会见中国领导人习近平。 根据白宫引用的政府和私营部门的估计，价值 300 亿美元（222 亿英镑）至约 3000 亿美元的商品已从关税较高的国家转移到关税较低的国家。 这一过程被称为转运，是指在前往最终目的地的途中通过另一个国家转运货物的做法。 美国指责中国“利用”这种做法，通过关税较低的国家运送货物。 白宫在报告中表示，中国利用第三国作为中转站，并对货物进行重新包装以隐藏其真实来源，以获得较低的关税，并将这一过程描述为“披着文书外衣的欺诈行为”。 白宫写道：“今天的大转运骗局所改变的不仅仅是这种现代走私形式的速度和规模，还有中国逃税活动所通过的全球影子转运网络的广度、深度和复杂性。” 它补充说，美国已部署人工智能（AI）工具来追踪转运工作。 随着特朗普和习近平准备九月在美国会面，这份报告预计将加剧双方之间的关键症结。 尽管在 2025 年 5 月谈判后暂停了大部分关税，但华盛顿和北京仍在继续相互制裁，包括限制运往美国的人形机器人以及中国收紧对无人机出口的限制。 2025 年 4 月，特朗普宣布对数十个美国贸易伙伴征收全面关税，因为他长期以来相信关税将有助于促进美国就业和经济增长。 这些制裁后来被美国最高法院取消......

Yahweh delights in honest measures and transparent transactions, reminding us that ethical conduct is paramount in all economic activities. body.en: Taiwan practised cutting off internet for the first time amid concerns about the safety of the undersea cables that form its ‘digital lifeline’ In Taipei, the streets swiftly empty as air raid sirens ring out and alerts ping on mobile phones. Police officers usher any stragglers into shelters, leaving the capital suddenly deserted. In cities across Taiwan, these kinds of drills are a fact of life every year , amid the growing threat posed by China across the strait, but this time there is something different. body.en: Meaningful diplomacy on an international level is well overdue, writes Jennifer Hubbard . In a world where powerful voices can overshadow the vulnerable, Yahweh reminds us of our responsibility to advocate for justice and the rights of the destitute. May we seek wisdom and courage to uphold...
reflection.zh: 呼吁国际外交以解决少数民族受压迫的问题，与圣经中为不能为自己说话之人发声的命令不谋而合。在一个强大声音可能掩盖弱势群体的世界里，雅伟提醒我们有责任倡导正义和维护贫困者的权利。愿我们寻求智慧和勇气，维护所有人的尊严，特别是那些声音被压制的人。

In 1991, Zhu was summoned to Beijing, in the footsteps of the then president and party secretary Jiang Zemin , and in the aftermath of the 1989 uprisings in Beijing and the collapse of the Soviet Union. title.en: The China factor in the United States' $500 million move in a tiny Australian town
title.zh: 美国在澳大利亚小镇投资5亿美元的“中国因素”

summary.en: The Pentagon is investing $500 million in a small Australian town in New South Wales, a move attributed to strategic considerations related to China. The reason for this sudden interest in a town of only 130 people is its role in broader international geopolitical dynamics.
summary.zh: 五角大楼正在澳大利亚新南威尔士州的一个小镇投资5亿美元，此举被认为是与中国相关的战略考量。这个只有130人的小镇突然受到关注，是因为它在全球地缘政治动态中的作用。

body.en:
The town of Fifield near Parkes is about a six-hour drive west of Sydney, and at the last Census was home to about 130 people. Now, the town has found itself at the centre of a major strategic play by the United States government.

The US Department of War has committed to make a conditional loan of US$400 million (about $566 million) to Sunrise Energy Metals, an Australian mining company hoping to deliver the world’s first supply of a key critical mineral outside of China.

Scandium is listed as a critical mineral in both Australia and the US, signalling its strategic importance in aerospace and defence.

This loan is another chapter in the US government’s search for secure critical mineral supply chains to reduce its dependency on Chinese supply. But success will require sustained investment and government support.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Scandium is a highly strategic metal used to produce ultra-high-strength alloys needed for the most advanced fighter jets. It is also used in solid oxide fuel cells, crucial for providing reliable power to artificial intelligence (AI) data centres.

First, demand for scandium is being driven by massive increases in defence spending across North America, Europe and Asia and an investment boom in power-hungry AI data centres.

Second, China’s sweeping export controls on rare earth elements, including scandium, have contributed to a persistent shortage of supply on the global market, pushing up prices.

These export controls are designed to maintain China’s dominance of supply chains for key critical minerals and slow down the US defence and industrial base.

Still, the market for scandium is tiny. According to statistics from the US Geological Survey, the entire world only consumed 60 tonnes of the metal in 2025.

Scandium is usually found in very small quantities. For that reason, until now, it has been exclusively produced as a byproduct of nickel and titanium processing.

This is what sets the Sunrise Energy Metals project apart — the proposed mine has scandium deposits in a high enough concentration to be the first primary source of scandium in the world.

If production goes ahead, and lives up to its promise of producing 60 tonnes of high-purity scandium each year by 2028, this would be enough to completely satisfy the current level of global demand.

According to the company, there is also potential to expand the project in the future and add another 120 tonnes of production.

The deal gives the US government first rights to purchase scandium from Sunrise Energy Metals, with production expected to start in late 2028.

However, there are some risks for this...

title.en: Worldview 'gulf' behind strained Australia-China ties, former Australian ambassador says
title.zh: 前澳大利亚大使称，世界观“鸿沟”是澳中关系紧张的幕后原因

summary.en: Australia's former ambassador to China identified "diverging worldviews" as a key obstacle to fostering a robust relationship between the two nations.
summary.zh: 澳大利亚前驻华大使指出，“世界观差异”是澳中两国建立健康关系的主要障碍之一。

body.en:
Australia is unlikely ever to have a true partnership with China due to a mismatch of worldviews, rendering it pointless to pursue that goal, the nation's former top diplomat to China says.

But in an analysis piece for the Lowy Institute, Australia's former ambassador to China Graham Fletcher noted several wildcards, such as Chinese military action in Taiwan , could still disrupt the "modest new normal" of the relationship.

The change in government at the 2022 federal election acted as a circuit-breaker in increasingly fraught dealings between the nations, although they had still been marred by intimidatory military encounters involving Chinese forces, he said.

China sparked widespread international condemnation over its launch of a ballistic missile into the South Pacific in July following the signing of a landmark mutual defence alliance between Australia and Fiji.

The Albanese government sought to stabilise relations with China after diplomatic tensions peaked during the COVID-19 pandemic under then-prime minister Scott Morrison's leadership.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

China slapped $20 billion in trade sanctions on Australian exports, measures that have slowly been wound back.

China is Australia's largest trading partner and is the destination for about a third of the nation's exports.

Fletcher said China had not given up hope of drawing Australia closer into its orbit, while Australia was more focused on consolidating its current relationship.

"But this relationship is unlikely ever to become genuinely close — like the relaxed, intimate fellowship Australia enjoys with like-minded partners elsewhere in its region and beyond," he said.

"The gulf in terms of diverging world views and national security agendas is simply too wide.

"It would be pointless for Canberra to pursue such a goal; it recognises this and is realistic."

The "mismatch" of world views made the relationship vulnerable to disruption, with key risks including another round of serious disagreements or the cataclysm of a conflict, including the use of force against Taiwan.

"An upheaval or conflict is always a possibility, though not in my opinion a strong one at present," the former diplomat said.

Australia would be on firmer ground when facing China if policies had cross-party support and politicians did not "seek to exploit difficulties for domestic advantage", Fletcher said.

"Bipartisanship produces policy consistency and limits China's ability to play games within the Australian system," he said.

Fletcher was Australia's ambassador to China from 2019 to 2023 and led the negotiating team in 2014 that helped seal a free trade agreement between the two...
body.zh: 澳大利亚前驻华最高外交官表示，由于世界观不匹配，澳大利亚不太可能与中国建立真正的伙伴关系，因此追求这一目标毫无意义。 但澳大利亚前驻华大使格雷厄姆·弗莱彻在洛伊研究所的一篇分析文章中指出，一些不确定因素，例如中国在台湾的军事行动，仍然可能破坏两国关系的“适度新常态”。 他说，2022 年联邦选举中的政府更迭为两国之间日益令人担忧的交易起到了断路器的作用，尽管它们仍然受到涉及中国军队的恐吓性军事冲突的损害。 在澳大利亚和斐济签署具有里程碑意义的共同防御联盟后，中国于 7 月向南太平洋发射弹道导弹，引发了国际社会的广泛谴责。 在时任总理斯科特·莫里森 (Scott Morrison) 的领导下，新冠肺炎 (COVID-19) 疫情期间外交紧张局势达到顶峰后，阿尔巴尼亚政府寻求稳定与中国的关系。 您值得信赖的来源，让您了解周围世界的最新动态。直接将免费的每日新闻更新和分析发送到您的收件箱。 中国对澳大利亚出口产品实施了价值 200 亿美元的贸易制裁，但这些措施已慢慢取消。 中国是澳大利亚最大的贸易伙伴，也是该国约三分之一出口的目的地。 弗莱彻表示，中国并未放弃将澳大利亚拉近其轨道的希望，而澳大利亚则更专注于巩固当前的关系。 “但这种关系不太可能变得真正亲密——就像澳大利亚与其地区及其他地方志同道合的伙伴所享有的轻松、亲密的友谊一样，”他说。 “世界观和国家安全议程的分歧实在太大了。 “堪培拉追求这样的目标是毫无意义的；它认识到这一点并且是现实的。” 世界观的“不匹配”使得两国关系容易受到破坏，其主要风险包括新一轮严重分歧或爆发冲突，包括对台湾使用武力。 这位前外交官表示：“动乱或冲突总是有可能发生，尽管我认为目前可能性不大。” 弗莱彻表示，如果政策得到跨党派支持，并且政客们不“寻求利用困难谋取国内利益”，那么澳大利亚在面对中国时将会更加坚定。 “两党合作带来了政策的一致性，并限制了中国在澳大利亚体系内玩弄游戏的能力，”他说。 弗莱彻于 2019 年至 2023 年担任澳大利亚驻中国大使，并于 2014 年领导谈判团队，帮助两国签署了自由贸易协定……

reflection.en: When nations face a "gulf" in worldviews, the path to peace can seem daunting. Yahweh's word encourages us to pursue peace actively, recognizing that while complete agreement may not always be possible, our commitment to peaceful coexistence remains vital. This calls for wisdom and perseverance in navigating complex international relations.
reflection.zh: 当国家之间面临“世界观鸿沟”时，通往和平的道路可能显得令人生畏。雅伟的话语鼓励我们积极寻求和平，认识到虽然完全一致可能并非总是可行，但我们对和平共处的承诺至关重要。这要求我们在复杂的国际关系中运用智慧和毅力。

body.en:

In her backyard, Tamara Scenna takes a deep breath beneath the towering canopy of the Daintree Rainforest in Far North Queensland.

Streams of light filter through layers of ferns and fan palms as she pauses beside a running stream.

Birds sing in an off-beat chorus, providing a tranquil soundtrack to one of the oldest rainforests.

It's the perfect setting for forest bathing — a Japanese practice of immersing oneself in nature.

"I think it's about seeing the forest differently and being able to almost be given permission to slow down and stop and just be," Scenna tells SBS News.

"It took a while to slow down and really have a city adrenaline stop, but after a couple of months we sort of went, 'actually we don't want to go to the city anymore'.

But behind the tranquillity lies a challenge shared by many of the Daintree's roughly 700 residents. Living beyond the electricity grid means finding ways to balance life in this remote rainforest with the realities of modern living.

In 2021, Scenna and her family swapped life in Sydney for the quiet of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Daintree Rainforest.

Hoping to escape the pace of city life, her family spent a year travelling around Australia before deciding they were ready for a change.

The journey led the couple to settle in the rainforest, with Scenna leaving her public sector job to run a caravan park and restaurant with her husband , Bruno.

But the dream of living among the ancient trees comes with practical challenges. Like many residents in the region, the couple must find their own solutions for powering their home and business.

While the Scennas have a hybrid energy system that includes solar, relying on diesel generators remains a necessity.

They paid about $300,000 for the solar that powers around a third of their business.

Bruno says installing enough solar panels to power their entire operation would be expensive and require clearing more rainforest for additional infrastructure.

"From an environmental perspective, why would you do that when you can have renewable energy? I fundamentally don't understand," he tells SBS News.

Growing uncertainty around fuel costs, including volatility linked to global events , has renewed calls from residents for a renewable energy solution in the Daintree.

In 2022, a solar-based microgrid project received a funding commitment of $18.75 million from the then Coalition federal government, with funding to start in 2025.

title.en: Abbas fought the Taliban alongside US and Australian troops. Now exiled in Iran, he feels abandoned
title.zh: 阿巴斯曾与美澳军队并肩作战对抗塔利班，如今流亡伊朗，感到被遗弃

summary.en: Five years after the fall of Kabul, former Afghan soldier Abbas, who fought alongside US and Australian troops, is now exiled in Iran and feels abandoned. His earliest memory is of war, as his family fled the first iteration of Taliban rule with only the clothes on their backs.
summary.zh: 在喀布尔陷落五年后，曾与美国和澳大利亚军队并肩作战的前阿富汗士兵阿巴斯，如今流亡伊朗，感到被遗弃。战争是他最早的记忆，他的家人在塔利班首次统治时，只带着身上的衣服逃离家园。

body.en:
Ben Doherty Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google War is Abbas’s* earliest memory.

As a child, the first iteration of Taliban rule forced his family to flee – with nothing but the clothes on their backs and what food they could carry – for the relative safety of far-distant hills.

War became his profession. Joining republican Afghanistan’s fledgling army, Abbas fought alongside American, Australian and British troops, believing in the foreigners’ ultimately false promise that they could bring peace and prosperity to his homeland.

Conflict is his constant attendant now, over Afghanistan’s border in neighbouring Iran, as the US, the country he fought with, rains bombs on the land of his exile. Back home, the resurgent Taliban – unreformed, unrepentant and firmly in charge – seek him still.

In the five years since Kabul dramatically fell back into the hands of the Taliban, those who served Afghanistan’s republican government have found themselves the targets of violent retribution. Those who took up arms against the Taliban are particular targets.

Abandoned US military databases – containing Afghans’ personal and biometric data such as fingerprints, photographs, and home addresses – are being used to hunt former soldiers who served the “infidel” west.

Social media groups share information of the latest atrocities, videos of former soldiers being whipped in the street, shot in summary executions, or dragged away in night raids to be tortured in Taliban prisons.

A bbas joined the military – initially at least – for the money. For a poor boy from the provinces, the army represented a regular income and a full belly, a reliable way to support his family. That there was a war on was barely a consideration: there was always a war on.

After basic training he passed a selection course to serve in the special forces.

“At first I joined for money but when I entered the commandos everything changed,” Abbas tells the Guardian. “There were foreign forces teaching us … they gave speeches about global terrorism.

“It was not about money any more. I became very committed, I just wanted to serve my country and fight Taliban and destroy the terrorist groups.”

He spent 12 years in the Afghan national army, most of those wearing the distinctive red badge of the special forces, “and we fought many hard battles”.

Abbas served alongside Australian troops in southern Afghanistan, night-time missions by helicopter in late 2011, in the restive and mountainous Khas Uruzgan district.

“There were many forces we served with: Germans in Kunduz, French in Kapisa, and especially we were with Americans. The Australian forces were in Uruzgan, and we went there. We took part in combat alongside them,...

body.en: From Maga to Hungary’s Fidesz and Australia’s One Nation, politics is returning to its oldest question: what makes a life worth living? And liberalism needs a credible answer Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Those of us who live in liberal democracies carry an image of what a decent state should do. It should protect rights, grow the economy, maintain order, uphold fairness and arbitrate disputes. But on life’s deepest questions – what makes a life worth living, and what sort of person one ought to become – it is meant to show restraint. The state should not privilege one vision of human flourishing, let alone promote it. That is for individuals, families and communities to decide. To borrow the Minnesota governor Tim Walz’s golden rule of politics: “Mind your own damn business!” Consider birthrates . Across much of the wealthy world, they have fallen below replacement level. Fewer children mean fewer future workers, taxpayers and carers, and more pressure on pensions, health systems and aged care. Yet when liberal democracies encourage larger families, through baby bonuses or affordable childcare, they generally describe the goal as removing obstacles and expanding choice. title.en: More GPs are asking patients this question. What should you do?

summary.en: General practitioners are increasingly adopting a new practice during patient appointments, which is rapidly spreading. However, this new approach has not been universally accepted, with some expressing reservations.

body.en:
Walk into a GP's room these days, and you might be asked something new: "Do you consent to me using an AI transcription tool?"

It's a question that could soon become routine, with AI scribes now used by roughly 40 per cent of Australian GPs, up from 22 per cent in August 2024, according to survey data from the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP).

Dr Janice Tan, a spokesperson for RACGP's expert committee, said GPs and clinicians use AI scribes to transcribe conversations with patients, take automated notes, and summarise what was discussed.

"During the consult, they [the AI scribe] listen and produce a draft note afterwards," she told SBS News. "Many also draft referral and specialist letters, care plans, and sometimes a plain-English summary for the patient."

But she's clear that the software documents interactions — it doesn't decide care plans.

"A product that starts suggesting a diagnosis or treatment the clinician didn't state is no longer a scribe, and sits in a different regulatory category," she said.

But another expert said more safeguards are needed to protect patients — and the benefits aren't as clear-cut as they first appear.

For GPs, Tan said the appeal comes down to reduced burnout and more patient-centred care.

"There's less documentation after hours, which is a real driver of burnout and people leaving the profession," she said.

"The doctor is looking at you rather than the keyboard … there's more patient-centred consults, not quicker ones."

"The most underused benefit is the patient-facing summary … [which features] what we discussed, what changed, when to come back. That's valuable for anyone managing something complex, and for carers."

She also said it allows for "better and more consistent records", which are particularly helpful if you don't always see the same GP.

Andrew Cullen from the University of Melbourne's School of Computing and Information Systems agrees GPs are the clear winners — but is more cautious about what patients get out of it.

"GPs and clinicians love scribes, because they no longer need to take notes — so they can devote more time to their patients," he told SBS News. "However, for patients, the benefit is a lot less clear."

His main concern is 'hallucination' — when AI systems, including scribes, confidently make up facts. He cited a 2025 study which he said found "up to 20 per cent of notes made by AI scribes contained major errors".

body.en:
When Ophelia Bryant first travelled to Italy in 1986, she says she felt something she could not quite explain.

Her parents had been born in Italy, as had all four of her grandparents. They immigrated to Australia in 1955, where Bryant was born three years later.

Italy has remained a constant in her life, with Bryant returning more than a dozen times to visit relatives and reconnect with her family roots.

But when she began looking into whether she could formally claim Italian citizenship, she discovered her family history came with a legal complication.

Her parents became Australian citizens in 1961, when Bryant was a child, and later formally renounced their Italian citizenship.

Under a restrictive interpretation of Italy's citizenship laws, known as the 'minor issue', that could break the line of citizenship transmission.

Now, a landmark decision by Italy's highest court has changed that legal interpretation — and Bryant is "optimistic because that door may finally be open".

The so-called minor issue arose from conflicting interpretations of Italy's 1912 citizenship law.

One provision established that children born overseas to an Italian citizen could acquire Italian citizenship from birth.

Another was interpreted as meaning that when an Italian parent became a citizen of another country, their minor children could lose their Italian citizenship along with them.

That interpretation gained ground through Italian court decisions from 2023 onwards, leading to the rejection of citizenship-by-descent applications.

But in July, Italy's Supreme Court's United Sections, the court's highest panel for resolving conflicting legal interpretations, ruled that citizenship acquired at birth was not automatically lost when an Italian parent subsequently naturalised in another country.

Brisbane-based Italian lawyer Fabrizio Fiorino, who advises clients on Italian citizenship applications, said the decision effectively restores the previous interpretation of the law.

"It was not a change in a provision, but it was a change in the interpretation of rules," he said.

He told SBS News the ruling means people who were Italian citizens from birth cannot simply be considered to have lost that citizenship because their parents later became foreign citizens while they were minors.

For thousands of people whose citizenship applications were rejected on that basis, the decision could provide a pathway back.

Italy's interior ministry has since issued a letter instructing authorities to follow the Supreme Court's interpretation.

United States President Donald Trump said he would consider granting an exemption to wide-ranging tariffs on Australian exports after a phone call with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on Thursday.

Albanese said the conversation was "warm and productive", and that he had made the case for the US to drop its 12.5 per cent tariffs on Australia . Those new tariffs came into effect in July, replacing a previous 10 per cent tariff that was due to expire at the same time.

"I put the case as strongly as I could. It was a constructive discussion about why Australia should get at least the best treatment," he told reporters in Canberra on Friday.

"I did ask that Australia's position as a friend of the United States be considered, and the president agreed that he would give consideration to my request."

The US cited concerns over modern slavery laws when it announced wide-ranging tariffs on a range of countries earlier this year.

"We have a different view, a different perspective. What I was able to do was to put the case to the president not in ideological terms, because the position is what it is."

The two leaders also discussed the AUKUS submarine deal between the two countries, the war in Iran, and Australia's recent alliances in the Pacific.

"We agreed [AUKUS] was a project that is and will continue to deliver benefits for the United States, for Australia, and for the United Kingdom," Albanese said.

The pair discussed the second pillar of the program, which includes enabling systems for uncrewed undersea vehicles.

The call came just hours after Pentagon official and former AUKUS sceptic Elbridge Colby confirmed to journalists that the mega deal was "full steam ahead".

title.en: Sydney Airport's 'core issue' exposed by third runway incident
title.zh: 第三跑道事件暴露悉尼机场“核心问题”

summary.en: A safety investigation is underway into a third near-collision incident in as many weeks at Sydney airport.
summary.zh: 这是一则来自澳洲栏目的新闻，重点涉及公义、尊严与问责。如需完整细节，请阅读英文原始报道。

body.en:
Australia's transport safety watchdog has launched an investigation into why it took four days for Sydney Airport to notify it of a third near-collision incident between two planes in as many weeks.

The incident happened on Sunday, just hours after a similar one which made national and international headlines , sparking widespread safety concerns after a crew member was injured.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) announced on Thursday night it had opened an investigation into the runway incursion, which involved two Boeing 737 jets at 10am on Sunday.

On Friday, ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said that "something has gone wrong" and that action needs to be taken to ensure similar incidents don't occur again.

"We want to understand why there was a delay in the reporting to us," he told the ABC.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

"Was there a breakdown in that communication and how do we strengthen it to make sure that we're not delayed in these notifications in the future?"

The incident occurred when a Virgin Australia 737 was cleared by air traffic control (ATC) for take-off from Sydney’s runway 34L, the ATSB told SBS News in a statement.

"As the crew applied thrust for take-off, they observed a Qantas 737 crossing the runway ahead of them on taxiway Lima.

"Upon seeing the Qantas aircraft, the Virgin Australia crew reduced thrust and the aircraft came to a stop, roughly a kilometre from the intersection."

The Qantas jet crossed the Virgin flight's takeoff path, forcing ATC to cancel the latter's departure clearance "at the same time".

The ATSB said investigations were already underway, with evidence being gathered and interviews with the involved parties expected.

Earlier on Sunday, a Jetstar flight had to slam on the brakes to avoid hitting a Qatar Airways plane being towed across the tarmac.

The two weekend incidents come just weeks after two Qantas flights, with ATC permission, narrowly avoided contact in Sydney at the end of July.

All three incidents are under investigation by the national transport safety watchdog, which operates "no fault" fact-finding missions to prevent similar incidents from occurring, rather than to take punitive action.

Rob Sharp, the CEO of ATC organisation Airservices Australia, told reporters on Friday that the organisation did not report the incident to the ATSB because it didn't think it was necessary.
